One of the latest numbers of Around the
World with Grant solves a problem which
has been a difficult conundrum heretofore.
Out in the China Seas General Grant gave the
only possible explanation we have seen of one


of the most incomprehensible movements
which followed the closing of the war. In
the mass of events which occurred in the
summer of 1865 it had been forgotten that an


army was massed in Southern and Southwest
Texas of at least 10000 men and under
able commanders. There was no enemy to
resist. The people of Texas were more
kindly than was the rule just after the sur-
render. General Merritt marched from
Shreveport to San Antonio, distance of 600


miles, with 6,000 cavalry under July
sun. Custer did the same with an
equal force on line about fifty miles
nearer the coast—two great invading forces,
and never shot was fired. What it was all
about the soldiers did not know. There was
no enemy in front, rear or flank, and instead
of living on the country, the country lived on
the army. All was paid for.


What it was all about was something that
those in the command, however intelligent,


did not understand. There was nothing to
fight about. Custer marched 5000 veterans
down the coast. Merritt took the interior
route. Andrews, Steele and others massed in-


fantry on the Rio Grande. In all there was a
body of say 10000 troops holding country
that had no resistance to offer and was getting
rich from the parade. There was a theory,
developed by the statesman who sat at
night on the wagon tongue that all this grand
moving and massing of armies was sort of a
torchlight demonstration to show the power
of the Union and overawe Texas. But Texas
was willingly overawed, and emptied its corn
cribs, sold its mesquite grass and filled its
pockets with greenbacks, and seemed to ad-


mire the grandeur of the Union. Every hospi-
tality was extended, and it was a very happy
occasion. And it lasted for several joyous
months in a good climate. What it was all
about was not so obvious.


Merritt's command reached San Antonio on
the 1st of August after march of 600
miles endowed with peace that would have
done credit to a Sunday school excursion. On
the 1st of September General Sheridan arrived.
There was grand review, dinner, and the
next morning Sheridan went tearing away
for Eagle Pass, distance of 160 miles,
with relays of horses for his ambulance,
which had been sent in advance. Just
why the Lieutenant-General should be so anx-
ious to get to Eagle Pass was not quite obvious.


Two years afterward he was asked if he went
there to meet Juarez, the Republican Presi-
dent of Mexico. He said that he did so to
the Secretary of State. Maximilian was then
Emperor, but furthermore he said no word.
Now, all this mystery of the massing of
troops on the Rio Grande, or within easy
reach of the Mexican border, becomes clear
in the light of a chat with General Grant on the
China seas, as reported by Mr. Young, who we
are sure would tell only the truth. The story
is that Grant ordered these troops to Texas to
be behind the Juarez government and, if he
could carry his point in Washington, to drive
the Emperor Maximilian home. He went to
President Johnson and urged the plan. Secre-
tary Seward opposed it. Grant's theory was
that Maximilian was the sworn enemy of Re-
publicanism on this continent, that he had
done all he could in behalf of rebellion, de-


served flogging and we had the mastery, with
the whip in our hands. Seward objected that
it would bring on an unnecessary conflict or
war with France. Grant answered that
Louis Napoleon had been our deadliest enemy
during all the war of the rebellion, and that
France could not afford foreign war across
the seas. The position was all in our hands.

sought. It was the overthrow of Maximilian
and the secure establishment of the Mexican
republic. Compelled to retain large army,
he might as well use it in that direction as in
any other. Mexico would make an outlet for
the restive spirits of the South, such as they
did seek in Brazil and Mexico itself. And
finally foreign war with France would not
hurt anybody much, and would tend strongly
to consolidate the warring sections of the
Union. Grant was overruled but we now
know how it was that great armies were hurled
upon Texas after peace had been declared and,
so far as that grand State is concerned, loyalty
accepted. It is one of the unaccomplished
facts of history.

JUDGE DAVIS'S EMPHATIC DECISION.

HE HOLDS THAT OFFICERS ARE SERVANTS OF THE PEOPLE NOT OF THE MAJORITY THAT ELECTED THEM—A MANDAMUS AGAINST COUNTY CLERK GUMBLETON.

Judge Davis has decided that the committee of the Bar Association is entitled to peremptory mandamus against County Clerk Gumbleton to compel him to show the committee the books of fees and liens. The decision however, goes further, and holds that all books kept by executive officers must be open to examination. His opinion is as follows:

"This matter brought before the Court by motion founded upon petition and affidavits. It met at the outset by affidavits the part of the respondent. It is well settled practice that the Court on motion founded on affidavits has the most discretion as to the extent which it will supplement with affidavits from either both parties, or adopt other appropriate modes of satisfying itself whether the motion ought to be granted or denied. In the exercise of that discretion in this case, the Court has allowed both of the parties to bring before it all such papers the counsel of either have thought it proper to present, and, animated solely by the hope that what scanned to it to be unreasonable and useless contravened the statute, in order to succeed with the intention, it such examination were allowed, the respondent has reset to avail himself of such opportunity by affidavits on the part of the realtor, showing such refusal and on the part of the respondent, of the Court been received. Upon all the papers now before the Court I am reluctantly forced to conclude that the conduct of the respondent has been the worst since he has met with me not to permit the books to be examined to prevent such examination so far as to stop it. When the realtors made their first application to him under the statute they were not only not produced but their examination was refused.

The statute was then clearly violated and the realtors plainly denied to them. The subsequent written attempt at negotiations between the realtors and the respondent does not in my opinion affect the merits of the motion, founded upon the legal acts of the respondent because it is manifest that the delay of the respondent sending his letter was not after the 8 o'clock of the following day, and until after the realtors had prepared papers for this motion and were in town in the morning before the motion was made, the attempt to make such examination as he let the letter rendered to them show that his willingness and offer to have the books examined was held.

The duty of the respondent under the statute was too plain to admit of discussion. He chose not, for reasons difficult to understand, he stands as a public officer and denies rights to the realtors which the statute makes his explicit duty to allow. An officer in this country is the servant of the people; and whether his position be conferred by popular ballot or by the appointment of the other authority, this relation is not changed. An officer is never the representative of the majority; once he accepts the office and enters upon his duties, both by law and under the theory of our system of government, he is altogether due to the people and not to any other body or power. An officer who does not recognize this truth ought not to accept the service of office and, having accepted it, he sets himself above the law and against the spirit of our local institutions. The Court, with the kindest possible intentions, endeavored to relieve the respondent from censure of standing in that position he deliberately to assume and uphold. The remedy ought to be certain and peremptory.

It is urged that the Court ought under the circumstances of the case to grant an alternative mandamus, as is always the practice where a material question of fact remains to be tried. But in this case, how much an immaterial question is presented and if it were found in favor of the respondent would not affect the Court's judgment, from the duty of issuing the peremptory writ. For, if it were found that the respondent did by his letter tender an examination of the books in good faith, that fact would be outweighed since immediately, when such examination was sought, refused in an unjustifiable manner, his conduct disarmed the realtors of the rights which the peremptory refusal by himself and his attorney had conveyed them. They were entitled to a court relief, and upon all the papers although proceedings that have since occurred, to deny it, to the other questions in the case were disposed of by the former opinion, the peremptory writ is thereby granted, with costs as the proceedings incurred may be settled upon one day's notice.

Mr. Gumbleton was in conference with his counsel Edwin K. Meade, but as he could not be reached he and his counsel propose to await the further action of the Court. The Bar Association Committee held meeting. But due to give any opinion of its resolutions, except that it has given notice to the County Clerk that the order could be settled."
